paragraphs.heading: What the Precambrian is
paragraphs.text: The Precambrian is the early part of Earth's history that came before the present Phanerozoic Eon. It runs from Earth's formation, around 4.6 billion years ago, to the start of the Cambrian Period, around 538.8 million years ago, when creatures with hard shells first turned up in large numbers. It covers 88% of geologic time and holds three eons: the Hadean, the Archean and the Proterozoic. The name just means it came before the Cambrian, which is named after Cambria, the Latin name for Wales, where rocks of that age were first studied.

paragraphs.heading: An informal label
paragraphs.text: Geologists and paleontologists use the word when speaking generally, when they have no need to name a particular eon. The International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) regards it as an informal term, and so does the United States Geological Survey. Because it holds three eons, it is sometimes called a supereon, but the ICS does not define that word either.

paragraphs.heading: Why so little is known
paragraphs.text: Even though it makes up about eight-ninths of Earth's story, the Precambrian is poorly understood, and most of what we know has been found since the 1960s. Its fossil record is thinner than that of later times, and fossils such as stromatolites are of limited use for biostratigraphy. Many of its rocks have been so heavily metamorphosed that their origins are hidden, while others have been worn away by erosion or lie deep under younger layers.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's beginnings
paragraphs.text: Earth is thought to have pulled together from material orbiting the Sun around 4,543 million years ago. Soon after, a smaller planet called Theia may have struck it, knocking off material that went on to form the Moon. A stable crust seems to have existed by 4,433 million years ago, since zircon crystals from Western Australia have been dated to 4,404 ± 8 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: The first signs of life
paragraphs.text: Nobody has pinned down when life began. Carbon in 3.8-billion-year-old rocks from islands off western Greenland may come from living things, and Western Australia has yielded well-preserved microscopic bacterial fossils more than 3.46 billion years old. There is even evidence that life could have arisen more than 4.280 billion years ago. Complex many-celled organisms may have appeared as early as 2100 million years ago, but the earliest ones widely accepted as such come from the Ediacaran Period, a varied set of soft-bodied forms found around the world.

paragraphs.heading: Oxygen and ice
paragraphs.text: Oxygen was not a large part of the air until life that photosynthesises evolved and began releasing it in large amounts as a by-product. At first the oxygen combined with elements in the crust, mostly iron; only when those surfaces were used up did it build up into today's oxygen-rich air. Massive banded iron formations, laid down as iron oxides in older rocks, are the evidence. The Precambrian also saw several glacial periods, and the Sturtian-Varangian glaciation, around 850 to 635 million years ago, may have carried ice all the way to the equator, a state called a "Snowball Earth".

paragraphs.heading: Continents come and go
paragraphs.text: Plate movements this far back are hard to read from the rocks. Small early continents are generally thought to have existed before 4280 million years ago. Most of the land then gathered into a single supercontinent, Rodinia, around 1130 million years ago, and Rodinia broke apart around 750 million years ago.
